title: Replication & consistency math
description: Replication and consistency reps for the data-tier part of a system-design interview: how long a quorum write or a strong read waits for its acks, which reads must stay on the primary when freshness is required, the write load that read repair quietly adds, anti-entropy traffic with and without Merkle trees, point-in-time restore time (snapshot copy plus WAL replay), placing a consensus cluster across zones so that losing a whole zone keeps a majority, how long before a lagging replica breaches its staleness SLA, and the share of reads a replica serves stale. Every drill is whole-number arithmetic with the conversions named (86,400 s/day; per-mille = parts per thousand = x/1000), so you practise the reasoning, not the calculator.

exercises.title: Quorum latency: the k-th ack, not the last
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Three replicas acknowledge a write after 10, 40 and 120 ms. With a write quorum of 2, when does the write commit? And if we drop to w = 1 on a five-replica cluster, what does a strongly consistent read cost now?"

**Why it works.** A quorum operation completes when the k-th replica answers — the slower ones after it do not matter. With the ack times sorted ascending, the k-quorum latency is simply the k-th entry, at zero-based index k − 1. Reads and writes trade against each other: a read is only guaranteed to see the latest write when r + w > n, so the smallest strong read quorum is r = n − w + 1, whose latency sits at index n − w. Inputs: `sortedAckMs` is sorted ascending, k ≥ 1 and w ≤ n.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `quorumAckMs(sortedAckMs, k)` → `sortedAckMs[k − 1]`
- `strongReadAckMs(sortedAckMs, n, w)` → `sortedAckMs[n − w]` (the r = n − w + 1-th ack)

**Worked example.** Acks at [10, 40, 120] ms with a quorum of k = 2 → the 2nd ack → **40 ms**.

tests.name: acks 10, 40, 120 with k = 2 -> 40 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.quorumAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named quorumAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.quorumAckMs([10,40,120], 2), 40);

tests.name: k = 1 -> the fastest ack, 10 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.quorumAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named quorumAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.quorumAckMs([10,40,120], 1), 10);

tests.name: five acks with k = 3 -> 200 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.quorumAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named quorumAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.quorumAckMs([5,80,200,350,900], 3), 200);

tests.name: n = 3, w = 2 -> the strong read waits 40 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.strongReadAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named strongReadAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.strongReadAckMs([10,40,120], 3, 2), 40);

tests.name: w = 1 forces the read to wait for every replica -> 900 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.strongReadAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named strongReadAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.strongReadAckMs([5,80,200,350,900], 5, 1), 900);

tests.name: n = 5, w = 4 -> the read needs 2 acks, 80 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.strongReadAckMs, 'function', 'export a function named strongReadAckMs');
assert.equal(mod.strongReadAckMs([5,80,200,350,900], 5, 4), 80);

exercises.explanation:
The quorum size is the index into the sorted acks.

For `strongReadAckMs([5, 80, 200, 350, 900], 5, 1)`:
- strong read quorum r = n − w + 1 = 5 − 1 + 1 = 5
- the 5th ack sits at index n − w = 4 → **900 ms**

A cheap write quorum is paid for at read time — module 03's `quorum-check` decides who must answer; this drill prices how long they take.
hints: A quorum is done the moment its k-th member answers; sort the acks and the slower replicas after that position stop mattering.
quorum latency = sorted[k − 1]; strong read: r = n − w + 1, so latency = sorted[n − w].
The k-th fastest ack arrives at sorted position k − 1, and a strong read needs r = n − w + 1 acks — index the sorted array at n − w for that latency

exercises.title: Routing fresh reads: what the primary really carries
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The app does 24,000 reads/s and 2,000 writes/s on one primary with async replicas; product says 25% of reads must see the latest write. What must the primary carry, and what may the replicas serve?"

**Why it works.** An async replica serves a slightly old view, so any read that must reflect the latest write has to go where the writes go. The primary therefore carries every write plus the fresh slice of reads; only the stale-tolerant remainder can be offloaded. Shares are in per-mille (‰ = x/1000). The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `primaryQps(writeQps, readQps, freshPermille)` → `writeQps + readQps × freshPermille ÷ 1000`
- `replicaQps(readQps, freshPermille)` → `readQps × (1000 − freshPermille) ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** 2,000 writes/s, 24,000 reads/s, 250‰ fresh → primary 2,000 + 6,000 = **8,000 QPS**; replicas serve 18,000.

tests.name: 2,000 writes + 25% of 24,000 reads -> 8,000 on the primary
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.primaryQps, 'function', 'export a function named primaryQps');
assert.equal(mod.primaryQps(2000, 24000, 250), 8000);

tests.name: no read needs the primary -> writes only (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.primaryQps, 'function', 'export a function named primaryQps');
assert.equal(mod.primaryQps(2000, 24000, 0), 2000);

tests.name: everything fresh -> replicas buy nothing (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.primaryQps, 'function', 'export a function named primaryQps');
assert.equal(mod.primaryQps(500, 10000, 1000), 10500);

tests.name: 24,000 reads at 250 permille fresh -> replicas serve 18,000
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.replicaQps, 'function', 'export a function named replicaQps');
assert.equal(mod.replicaQps(24000, 250), 18000);

tests.name: 1000 permille fresh -> replicas serve 0 (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.replicaQps, 'function', 'export a function named replicaQps');
assert.equal(mod.replicaQps(10000, 1000), 0);

tests.name: 30,000 reads at 100 permille fresh -> 27,000 offloaded
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.replicaQps, 'function', 'export a function named replicaQps');
assert.equal(mod.replicaQps(30000, 100), 27000);

exercises.explanation:
Read-your-writes belongs to the primary.

For `primaryQps(2000, 24000, 250)`:
- fresh reads: 24,000 × 250 ÷ 1000 = 6,000/s
- plus all 2,000 writes → **8,000 QPS** on the primary

Replicas only ever offload the stale-tolerant slice — if product demands 100% freshness, replicas buy nothing (module 10's replica sizing then applies to what is left).
hints: A read that must see the latest write cannot be answered by an async replica — it lands on the primary on top of every write.
primary = writeQps + readQps × fresh‰ ÷ 1000; replicas = readQps × (1000 − fresh‰) ÷ 1000.
Fresh reads must go where the writes land, so the primary carries writes plus the fresh per-mille slice of reads — the replicas get the remaining (1000 − fresh‰) slice

exercises.title: Read repair: the writes your reads create
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Reads run at 10,000/s and read repair compares 3 replicas on every read; 2% of those checks find a stale copy and write it back. Real client writes are 2,000/s. How many repair writes does read traffic create, and how big is that next to the real write load?"

**Why it works.** Read repair compares every copy a read touches and writes the fresh value back to any stale one. Checks per second are reads × replicasChecked, and the stale per-mille of those checks (‰ = x/1000) become repair writes — writes caused by READ traffic. Comparing that stream to the real write rate, again in per-mille, shows how much the read path amplifies the write path. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `repairWritesPerSec(readQps, replicasChecked, stalePermille)` → `readQps × replicasChecked × stalePermille ÷ 1000`
- `repairSharePermille(readQps, replicasChecked, stalePermille, writeQps)` → `repairWritesPerSec(readQps, replicasChecked, stalePermille) × 1000 ÷ writeQps`

**Worked example.** 10,000 reads/s × 3 copies checked × 20‰ stale → **600** repair writes/s.

tests.name: 10,000 reads x 3 copies at 20 permille stale -> 600 repairs/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairWritesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named repairWritesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.repairWritesPerSec(10000, 3, 20), 600);

tests.name: nothing stale -> 0 repairs (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairWritesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named repairWritesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.repairWritesPerSec(10000, 3, 0), 0);

tests.name: 5,000 reads x 2 copies at 50 permille stale -> 500 repairs/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairWritesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named repairWritesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.repairWritesPerSec(5000, 2, 50), 500);

tests.name: 600 repairs vs 2,000 writes/s -> 300 permille
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairSharePermille, 'function', 'export a function named repairSharePermille');
assert.equal(mod.repairSharePermille(10000, 3, 20, 2000), 300);

tests.name: repairs equal the real write load -> 1000 permille (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairSharePermille, 'function', 'export a function named repairSharePermille');
assert.equal(mod.repairSharePermille(5000, 2, 50, 500), 1000);

tests.name: 8,000 reads x 5 copies at 10 permille vs 4,000 writes/s -> 100 permille
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.repairSharePermille, 'function', 'export a function named repairSharePermille');
assert.equal(mod.repairSharePermille(8000, 5, 10, 4000), 100);

exercises.explanation:
Read repair turns a stale-read rate into write load.

For `repairSharePermille(10000, 3, 20, 2000)`:
- checks: 10,000 reads × 3 copies = 30,000/s
- repairs: 30,000 × 20 ÷ 1000 = 600 writes/s
- share: 600 × 1000 ÷ 2,000 = **300‰**

Read traffic quietly adds 30% to the write path — module 02's `missesPerSecond` applies one per-mille to reads, while here the replica fan-out multiplies the checks and the result lands on the WRITE side.
hints: Every read compares several copies, and each stale copy it finds is written back — those are writes your read traffic generates.
repairs = readQps × replicasChecked × stale‰ ÷ 1000; share‰ = repairs × 1000 ÷ writeQps.
Each read checks replicasChecked copies and the stale per-mille of those checks becomes a repair write — compare that repair stream to the real write rate by scaling with 1000 ÷ writeQps

exercises.title: Anti-entropy: full compare vs Merkle trees
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Each replica holds 1 GB and we keep 3 replicas. A nightly anti-entropy job compares one copy against each of the other replicas. How many bytes cross the network if it streams the full data set — and how many with Merkle trees, when only 0.5% of the key ranges actually diverge?"

**Why it works.** A naive full compare streams the whole data set to each of the replicas − 1 peers on every sync. Merkle (hash) trees let replicas exchange hashes first and stream only the ranges whose hashes differ, so the traffic shrinks to the divergent per-mille slice (‰ = x/1000). (Exchanging the hashes and the leaf-range granularity add some overhead; this drill sizes the streamed ranges only.) Conversions: 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `fullSyncBytesPerDay(dataBytes, replicas, syncsPerDay)` → `dataBytes × (replicas − 1) × syncsPerDay`
- `merkleSyncBytesPerDay(dataBytes, replicas, syncsPerDay, divergentPermille)` → `fullSyncBytesPerDay(dataBytes, replicas, syncsPerDay) × divergentPermille ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** 1 GB on 3 replicas synced once a day → 1,000,000,000 × 2 × 1 = **2,000,000,000 bytes** a day for the full compare.

tests.name: 1 GB, 3 replicas, 1 sync/day -> 2,000,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named fullSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay(1000000000, 3, 1), 2000000000);

tests.name: RF 1 has nothing to compare -> 0 bytes (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named fullSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay(1000000000, 1, 4), 0);

tests.name: 500 MB, 4 replicas, 2 syncs/day -> 3,000,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named fullSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.fullSyncBytesPerDay(500000000, 4, 2), 3000000000);

tests.name: Merkle at 5 permille divergent -> 10,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named merkleSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay(1000000000, 3, 1, 5), 10000000);

tests.name: fully divergent -> the trees save nothing (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named merkleSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay(1000000000, 3, 1, 1000), 2000000000);

tests.name: 500 MB, 4 replicas, 2 syncs at 10 permille -> 30,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named merkleSyncBytesPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.merkleSyncBytesPerDay(500000000, 4, 2, 10), 30000000);

exercises.explanation:
Replication factor multiplies repair traffic; divergence divides it.

For `merkleSyncBytesPerDay(1000000000, 3, 1, 5)`:
- naive compare: 1,000,000,000 bytes × 2 peers × 1 sync = 2,000,000,000 bytes/day
- Merkle slice: 2,000,000,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = **10,000,000 bytes** (~10 MB)

Hash trees narrow repair to the divergent ranges — unlike module 10's `physicalGb`, where RF multiplies storage at rest, here RF − 1 multiplies repair traffic and the Merkle factor cuts it back down.
hints: A replica reconciles against every other replica, and a full compare ships the whole data set each time — hash trees let it ship only what differs.
full = dataBytes × (replicas − 1) × syncs/day; merkle = full × divergent‰ ÷ 1000.
A full compare streams the data to each of the replicas − 1 peers every sync, so multiply those three — merkle trees cut that to the divergent per-mille slice, another ÷ 1000

exercises.title: Point-in-time restore: snapshot copy plus WAL replay
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The database is 600 GB, snapshotted every 12 hours, and takes 500 writes/s. Worst case, it dies just before the next snapshot. A restore copies at 200 MB/s and the write-ahead log replays at 12,000 events/s. How long until we are back?"

**Why it works.** Point-in-time recovery runs two phases one after the other: copy the last snapshot, then replay every write-ahead-log (WAL) event recorded since it. The WAL grows at the write rate for every second since the snapshot, so a 12-hour cadence (43,200 s) leaves writesPerSec × 43,200 events to replay in the worst case. Conversions: 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes, so 600 GB = 600,000,000,000 bytes and 200 MB/s = 200,000,000 bytes/s. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `walEventsToReplay(writesPerSec, secondsSinceSnapshot)` → `writesPerSec × secondsSinceSnapshot`
- `restoreSeconds(snapshotBytes, restoreBytesPerSec, walEvents, replayPerSec)` → `snapshotBytes ÷ restoreBytesPerSec + walEvents ÷ replayPerSec`

**Worked example.** 500 writes/s for 43,200 s since the snapshot → **21,600,000** WAL events to replay.

tests.name: 500 writes/s for 12 hours -> 21,600,000 events
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.walEventsToReplay, 'function', 'export a function named walEventsToReplay');
assert.equal(mod.walEventsToReplay(500, 43200), 21600000);

tests.name: crash right after the snapshot -> 0 events (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.walEventsToReplay, 'function', 'export a function named walEventsToReplay');
assert.equal(mod.walEventsToReplay(500, 0), 0);

tests.name: 2,000 writes/s for 1 hour -> 7,200,000 events
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.walEventsToReplay, 'function', 'export a function named walEventsToReplay');
assert.equal(mod.walEventsToReplay(2000, 3600), 7200000);

tests.name: 600 GB at 200 MB/s + 21,600,000 events at 12,000/s -> 4,800 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.restoreSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named restoreSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.restoreSeconds(600000000000, 200000000, 21600000, 12000), 4800);

tests.name: snapshot only -> 3,000 s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.restoreSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named restoreSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.restoreSeconds(600000000000, 200000000, 0, 12000), 3000);

tests.name: 100 GB at 100 MB/s + 3,000,000 events at 10,000/s -> 1,300 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.restoreSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named restoreSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.restoreSeconds(100000000000, 100000000, 3000000, 10000), 1300);

exercises.explanation:
Recovery time is two derived phases added together.

For `restoreSeconds(600000000000, 200000000, 21600000, 12000)`:
- copy: 600,000,000,000 bytes ÷ 200,000,000 bytes/s = 3,000 s
- replay: 21,600,000 events ÷ 12,000/s = 1,800 s
- total: 3,000 + 1,800 = **4,800 s** (80 minutes)

That is the real RTO behind "we have backups", and the snapshot cadence sets the second term — module 06's `pipelineLatencyMs` sums stage times it is given, while here both phases are derived from sizes and rates.
hints: A restore first copies the snapshot back, then re-applies every logged write since that snapshot — the two phases run in sequence.
walEvents = writes/s × seconds since snapshot; restore = snapshotBytes ÷ restoreBytes/s + walEvents ÷ replay/s.
Recovery is two phases added together: snapshot bytes ÷ restore throughput, plus WAL events ÷ replay rate — and the WAL grew at writesPerSec for every second since the snapshot

exercises.title: Replica lag: how long until the SLA breaks
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The primary writes 5,000 events/s but one replica only replays 4,200/s. It is already 100,000 events behind, and the staleness SLA breaks at 500,000. How long before it breaches — how much warning does the lag alert actually buy us?"

**Why it works.** Replication lag changes every second by the difference between what arrives and what the replica can replay: writeQps − replayQps. A positive difference grows the lag linearly, zero holds it steady, and a negative one means the replica is catching up. While it grows, the time until the lag hits the ceiling is the remaining headroom divided by that deficit. `breachSeconds` is only called with writeQps > replayQps and maxLagEvents > currentLagEvents. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `lagGrowthPerSec(writeQps, replayQps)` → `writeQps − replayQps` (may be negative: catching up)
- `breachSeconds(currentLagEvents, maxLagEvents, writeQps, replayQps)` → `(maxLagEvents − currentLagEvents) ÷ (writeQps − replayQps)`

**Worked example.** 5,000 writes/s against 4,200 replayed/s → the lag grows by **800** events every second.

tests.name: 5,000 writes vs 4,200 replayed -> lag grows 800/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.lagGrowthPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named lagGrowthPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.lagGrowthPerSec(5000, 4200), 800);

tests.name: treading water -> 0 growth (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.lagGrowthPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named lagGrowthPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.lagGrowthPerSec(3000, 3000), 0);

tests.name: replica faster than the writes -> -600/s, catching up
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.lagGrowthPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named lagGrowthPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.lagGrowthPerSec(2000, 2600), -600);

tests.name: 100,000 behind, ceiling 500,000, deficit 800/s -> 500 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.breachSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named breachSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.breachSeconds(100000, 500000, 5000, 4200), 500);

tests.name: starting even, ceiling 360,000, deficit 600/s -> 600 s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.breachSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named breachSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.breachSeconds(0, 360000, 3000, 2400), 600);

tests.name: 40,000 behind, ceiling 100,000, deficit 120/s -> 500 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.breachSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named breachSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.breachSeconds(40000, 100000, 4000, 3880), 500);

exercises.explanation:
A replica that cannot keep up turns a rate gap into a countdown.

For `breachSeconds(100000, 500000, 5000, 4200)`:
- deficit: 5,000 − 4,200 = 800 events/s
- headroom: 500,000 − 100,000 = 400,000 events
- time to breach: 400,000 ÷ 800 = **500 s**

Roughly eight minutes of warning before the staleness SLA dies — module 06's `drainSeconds` is the surplus case where a backlog shrinks to zero, and this is its deficit mirror: time until a growing lag hits a ceiling.
hints: Each second the primary adds writeQps events and the replica removes replayQps of them — the lag moves by the difference.
growth = writeQps − replayQps; t = (maxLag − currentLag) ÷ (writeQps − replayQps).
The lag grows at writeQps − replayQps each second, so divide the remaining headroom (maxLag − currentLag) by that deficit for the seconds until breach

exercises.title: Stale reads: lag over update interval
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A product price is rewritten every 10 seconds and the replicas lag the primary by 200 ms. What share of replica reads return the old price? And if product tolerates at most 5% stale reads on a value updated once a minute, how much lag may we accept?"

**Why it works.** After each write a replica keeps serving the old value for lagMs, then holds the new one until the next write. With reads spread evenly over time, the stale share is lagMs out of every updateIntervalMs — in per-mille (‰ = x/1000), lagMs × 1000 ÷ updateIntervalMs. Inverting that turns a staleness budget into the largest lag you may tolerate. The lag is never longer than the update interval. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `stalePermilleOfReads(lagMs, updateIntervalMs)` → `lagMs × 1000 ÷ updateIntervalMs`
- `maxLagMsForBudget(budgetPermille, updateIntervalMs)` → `budgetPermille × updateIntervalMs ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** A 50‰ budget on a value updated every 60,000 ms → 50 × 60,000 ÷ 1000 = **3,000 ms** of tolerable lag.

tests.name: 200 ms lag on a 10 s update cycle -> 20 permille stale
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.stalePermilleOfReads, 'function', 'export a function named stalePermilleOfReads');
assert.equal(mod.stalePermilleOfReads(200, 10000), 20);

tests.name: no lag -> 0 permille (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.stalePermilleOfReads, 'function', 'export a function named stalePermilleOfReads');
assert.equal(mod.stalePermilleOfReads(0, 5000), 0);

tests.name: lag equals the update interval -> every read window stale (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.stalePermilleOfReads, 'function', 'export a function named stalePermilleOfReads');
assert.equal(mod.stalePermilleOfReads(5000, 5000), 1000);

tests.name: 50 permille budget on 60 s updates -> 3,000 ms of lag
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxLagMsForBudget, 'function', 'export a function named maxLagMsForBudget');
assert.equal(mod.maxLagMsForBudget(50, 60000), 3000);

tests.name: 1000 permille budget on 2 s updates -> 2,000 ms of lag
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxLagMsForBudget, 'function', 'export a function named maxLagMsForBudget');
assert.equal(mod.maxLagMsForBudget(1000, 2000), 2000);

tests.name: 10 permille budget on 30 s updates -> 300 ms of lag
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxLagMsForBudget, 'function', 'export a function named maxLagMsForBudget');
assert.equal(mod.maxLagMsForBudget(10, 30000), 300);

exercises.explanation:
The stale share is the lag's slice of each update cycle.

For `stalePermilleOfReads(200, 10000)`:
- each 10,000 ms cycle is stale for its first 200 ms
- 200 × 1000 ÷ 10,000 = **20‰** of uniformly spread reads see the old value

Run it backwards and a staleness budget becomes a lag SLO — module 03's `replication-staleness` counts one lag window's reads through the quorum check, while here the steady-state share comes from lag ÷ update interval.
hints: Picture one update cycle: the replica is wrong only for the lag right after each write and right for the rest of the cycle.
stale‰ = lagMs × 1000 ÷ intervalMs; maxLag = budget‰ × intervalMs ÷ 1000.

A value updated every interval is stale on the replica for lagMs after each write, so the stale share of reads is lag × 1000 ÷ interval — invert it to turn a staleness budget into the lag you may tolerate

exercises.title: Quorum placement: surviving the loss of a whole zone
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our 5-node Raft cluster has to survive an availability-zone outage. Do we spread it over 2 zones (3 + 2) or over 3 zones (2 + 2 + 1)? And would a 4-node cluster over 2 zones do?"

**Why it works.** A consensus cluster keeps working only while a majority of its nodes, ⌊nodes ÷ 2⌋ + 1, is alive. Nodes in one zone fail together, so the failure to plan for is the loss of the BIGGEST zone. Spread as evenly as possible, the biggest zone holds ⌈nodes ÷ zones⌉ nodes, and the cluster survives the zone outage only if the nodes left over still form a majority. Inputs: nodes ≥ 1 and zones ≥ 1, and the nodes are always spread as evenly as possible.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss(nodes, zones)` → the nodes still running after the biggest zone is lost
- `survivesZoneLoss(nodes, zones)` → `true` when those survivors are still a majority of `nodes`, otherwise `false`

**Worked example.** 5 nodes over 3 zones (2 + 2 + 1) → losing a 2-node zone leaves **3** running, and 3 is a majority of 5.

tests.name: 5 nodes over 3 zones, lose a 2-node zone -> 3 left
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss(5, 3), 3);

tests.name: 5 nodes over 2 zones, lose the 3-node zone -> 2 left
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss(5, 2), 2);

tests.name: 3 nodes in a single zone -> 0 left (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.nodesLeftAfterZoneLoss(3, 1), 0);

tests.name: 5 nodes over 3 zones -> survives the zone loss
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.survivesZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named survivesZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.survivesZoneLoss(5, 3), true);

tests.name: 5 nodes over 2 zones -> 2 of 5 is no majority, false
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.survivesZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named survivesZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.survivesZoneLoss(5, 2), false);

tests.name: 4 nodes split 2 + 2 -> half is not a majority, false
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.survivesZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named survivesZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.survivesZoneLoss(4, 2), false);

tests.name: 3 nodes, one per zone -> 2 of 3 survive (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.survivesZoneLoss, 'function', 'export a function named survivesZoneLoss');
assert.equal(mod.survivesZoneLoss(3, 3), true);

exercises.explanation:
A zone is one failure, however many nodes it holds.

For `survivesZoneLoss(5, 2)`:
- the biggest zone holds ⌈5 ÷ 2⌉ = 3 nodes, so losing it leaves 5 − 3 = 2
- the majority of 5 is ⌊5 ÷ 2⌋ + 1 = 3
- 2 < 3 → **false**: the cluster stops accepting writes

Spread evenly over two zones the survivors are at most half the cluster, so no node count makes two zones safe — that is why etcd, ZooKeeper and Raft databases run across three zones (or two plus a tie-breaker). Module 03's `quorum-check` counts node failures one at a time; this drill counts the correlated failure of a whole zone.
hints: Nodes in the same zone go down together — ask what is left when the biggest zone disappears, and whether that is still more than half.
left = nodes − ⌈nodes ÷ zones⌉; survives ⇔ left ≥ ⌊nodes ÷ 2⌋ + 1.

Spread evenly, the biggest zone holds the node count divided by the zone count rounded up — subtract that from the cluster and compare what is left with the majority, half the nodes rounded down plus one
